danish.title: Femte bog (1806–07) — Kapitel 15
paragraphs: Da Rostov vendte tilbage fra sin orlov, mærkede han for første gang, hvor tæt det bånd var, der bandt ham til Denisov og hele regimentet.

Da han nærmede sig, følte Rostov det samme, som da han nærmede sig sit hjem i Moskva. Da han genkendte den første husar i sit regiments uknappede uniform, da han genkendte rødhårede Dementjev og så de roan-farvede hestes tøjrepæle, da Lavrusjka jublende råbte til sin herre: »Greven er kommet!«, og Denisov, der havde sovet på sin seng, kom løbende helt forpjusket ud af jordhytten for at omfavne ham, og officererne samledes for at hilse på den nyankomne — da oplevede Rostov den samme følelse, som da hans mor, hans far og hans søster havde omfavnet ham, og glædestårer snørede sig om hans strube, så han ikke kunne tale. Regimentet var også et hjem, og et lige så urokkelig kært og dyrebart hjem som hans forældres hus.

Da han havde meldt sig til regimentschefen og fået sin gamle eskadron tildelt igen, havde været på vagt og havde været ude at fouragere, da han på ny var trådt ind i regimentets små interesser og følte sig berøvet sin frihed og bundet i én snæver, uforanderlig ramme — oplevede han den samme følelse af fred, af moralsk støtte og af at være hjemme på sin egen plads, som han havde følt under forældrenes tag. Men her var der intet af hele den vide verdens tumult, hvor han ikke kendte sin rette plads og tog fejlagtige beslutninger; her var der ingen Sonja, som han burde eller ikke burde have en forklaring med; her var der ingen mulighed for at tage derhen eller lade være; her var der ikke fire og tyve timer i døgnet, der kunne bruges på så mange forskellige måder; her var der ikke den utallige skare af mennesker, af hvem ingen stod ham nærmere eller fjernere end nogen anden; her var der ingen af de usikre og uklare pengesager med hans far, og intet der mindede om det forfærdelige tab til Dolokhov. Her i regimentet var alt klart og enkelt. Hele verden var delt i to ulige dele: den ene var vores Pavlogradske regiment; den anden alt det øvrige. Og det øvrige kom ham ikke ved. I regimentet var alt bestemt: hvem der var løjtnant, hvem der var kaptajn, hvem der var en god kammerat, og hvem der ikke var, og først og fremmest hvem der var en kammerat. Kantinebestyreren gav kredit, lønnen kom hver fjerde måned, der var intet at tænke over eller beslutte — man skulle bare undlade at gøre noget, der blev anset for dårligt i Pavlogradregimentet, og når man fik en ordre, gøre det der tydeligt, bestemt og klart var befalet — og alt var godt.

Da Rostov atter var trådt ind i dette regimentslivs faste rammer, følte han den glæde og lettelse, en træt mand føler, når han lægger sig til at hvile. Livet i regimentet var under dette felttog desto behageligere for ham, fordi han efter sit tab til Dolokhov — som han trods hele familiens forsøg på at trøste ham ikke kunne tilgive sig selv — havde besluttet at sone sin fejl ved at tjene, ikke som han havde gjort før, men virkelig godt, og ved at være en aldeles førsteklasses kammerat og officer — kort sagt et pragtfuldt menneske i det hele taget, noget der syntes så vanskeligt ude i verden, men så muligt i regimentet.

Efter sine tab havde han besluttet at betale sin gæld til forældrene tilbage på fem år. Han modtog ti tusind rubler om året, men besluttede nu kun at beholde to tusind og lade resten gå til at betale gælden af.
Vores hær havde efter gentagne tilbagetræk-ninger, fremrykninger og slag ved Pultusk og Preussisch-Eylau samlet sig nær Bartenstein. Den ventede kejserens ankomst og begyndelsen på et nyt felttog.

Pavlogradregimentet, der hørte til den del af hæren, der havde tjent i 1805-felttoget, havde rekrutteret op til fuld styrke i Rusland og var ankommet for sent til at deltage i felttogenes første kampe. Det havde hverken været med ved Pultusk eller Preussisch-Eylau og blev, da det stødte til hæren i felten i anden halvdel af felttoget, tilknyttet Platovs division.

Platovs division opererede uafhængigt af hovedhæren. Flere gange havde dele af Pavlogradregimentet udvekslet skud med fjenden, taget fanger, og én gang endda erobret marskal Oudinots vogne. I april lå Pavlograderne ubevægeligt stationeret i nogle uger nær en fuldstændig ødelagt og forladt tysk landsby.

Tøvejr var sat ind, det var mudret og koldt, isen på floden brød op, og vejene blev ufremkommelige. I dagevis var der hverken blevet uddelt forsyninger til mandskabet eller foder til hestene. Da ingen transporter kunne komme frem, spredte soldaterne sig ud i de forladte og øde landsbyer på jagt efter kartofler, men fandt kun få selv af dem.

Alt var blevet spist op, og beboerne var alle flygtet — og de få, der var tilbage, var værre end tiggere, og der var intet mere at tage fra dem; ja, soldaterne, som ellers var hensynsløse nok, gav dem ofte det sidste af deres egne rationer i stedet for at tage noget.

Pavlogradregimentet havde kun haft to mand såret i kamp, men havde mistet næsten halvdelen af sit mandskab af sult og sygdom. På hospitalerne var døden så sikker, at soldater med feber eller den hævelse, der kom af dårlig kost, foretrak at blive ved fronten og næsten ikke kunne slæbe benene med sig frem for at gå i tjeneste snarere end at komme på hospital. Da foråret kom, fandt soldaterne en plante, der netop stak frem af jorden og lignede asparges, som de af en eller anden grund kaldte »Masjkas søde rod«. Den var meget bitter, men de strejfede rundt på markerne og ledte efter den, gravede den op med deres sabler og spiste den, skønt de havde fået forbud mod det, da det var en giftig plante. Det forår brød en ny sygdom ud blandt soldaterne, en hævelse af arme, ben og ansigt, som lægerne tilskrev indtagelsen af denne rod. Men trods alt dette levede soldaterne i Denisovs eskadron hovedsageligt af »Masjkas søde rod«, for det var nu den anden uge, de sidste beskøjter blev uddelt med en halv pund pr. mand, og de sidst modtagne kartofler havde spiret og var frosne.
Hestene havde i to uger fået halm fra stråtagene som foder og var blevet forfærdeligt magre, men var stadig dækkede af totter af filtet vinterpels.

Trods denne elendighed levede soldater og officerer videre som sædvanligt. Trods deres blege, opsvulmede ansigter og lasede uniformer stillede husarerne op til navneopråb, holdt tingene i orden, pudsede deres våben, bragte halm fra stråtagene i stedet for foder og satte sig til bords ved kedlerne, som de rejste sig sultne fra, mens de jokede om deres modbydelige mad og deres sult. Som altid tændte de bål i deres fritid, dampbadede sig nøgne foran dem, røg, plukkede og stegte spirende, rådne kartofler, fortalte og lyttede til historier om Potemkins og Suvorovs felttog eller til sagn om Aljosha den Snedige eller om præstens karl Mikolka.

Officererne boede som sædvanligt to og tre sammen i de tagløse, halvødelagte huse. De ældre forsøgte at skaffe halm og kartofler og i det hele taget mad til mandskabet. De yngre beskæftigede sig som før, nogle med kortspil — der var rigeligt med penge, selv om der ingen mad var — nogle med mere uskyldige spil som quoits og keglespil. Om felttogenes gang talte man sjældent, dels fordi intet sikkert var kendt derom, dels fordi der var en vag fornemmelse af, at det i hovedtræk gik dårligt.

Rostov levede som før sammen med Denisov, og siden deres orlov var de blevet endnu tættere knyttet til hinanden. Denisov talte aldrig om Rostovs familie, men ud fra den ømme venskabelighed, hans kommandør viste ham, følte Rostov, at den ældre husars ulykkelige kærlighed til Natasja spillede en rolle i styrkelsen af deres venskab. Denisov forsøgte tydeligvis at udsætte Rostov for fare så sjældent som muligt og hilste efter en træfning hans sikre hjemkomst med synlig glæde. Under en af sine fouragerings-ekspeditioner i en forladt og ødelagt landsby, hvor han var kommet hen for at lede efter forsyninger, fandt Rostov en familie bestående af en gammel polak og hans datter med et spædbarn i armene. De var halvnøgne, sultne, for svage til at komme af sted til fods og havde ingen mulighed for at skaffe befordring. Rostov bragte dem til sit kvarter, anbragte dem i sit eget logi og forsørgede dem i nogle uger, mens den gamle mand kom til kræfter. En af hans kammerater, som talte om kvinder, begyndte at drille Rostov og sagde, at han var mere snedig end nogen af dem, og at det ikke ville være dårligt, hvis han introducerede den smukke polske pige, han havde reddet, for dem. Rostov opfattede spøgen som en fornærmelse, brusede op og sagde så ubehagelige ting til officeren, at det var alt, hvad Denisov kunne gøre, for at forhindre en duel. Da officeren var gået, begyndte Denisov, der ikke selv vidste, hvad Rostovs forhold til den polske pige var, at skælde ham ud for hans opfarenhed, og Rostov svarede:
»Sig, hvad du vil... Hun er som en søster for mig, og jeg kan ikke fortælle dig, hvor fornærmet jeg blev... fordi... ja, af den grund.«
Denisov klappede ham på skulderen og begyndte hurtigt at vandre frem og tilbage i stuen uden at se på Rostov, som han plejede i øjeblikke med stærke følelser.
»Åh, sikke en tosset slægt, I Rostov'er er!« mumlede han, og Rostov lagde mærke til tårer i hans øjne.

english.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 15
paragraphs: When Rostov returned from leave to his regiment, he felt for the first time how strong the bond was that tied him to Denisov and the regiment as a whole.

As he approached, Rostov felt the same thing he'd felt when approaching his family home in Moscow. When he spotted the first hussar in the unbuttoned uniform of his regiment, when he recognized red-haired Dementyev and saw the picket ropes of the roan horses, when Lavrushka joyfully shouted to his master, "The count has come!" and Denisov, who'd been asleep, came running out of the mud hut all disheveled to embrace him, and the officers crowded around to greet the new arrival — Rostov felt the same emotion as when his mother, father, and sister had embraced him. Tears of joy choked him so that he couldn't speak. The regiment was also a home, and one as unchangeably dear and precious as his parents' house.

When he had reported to the regimental commander and been reassigned to his old squadron, when he'd been on duty and gone out foraging, when he had re-entered all the small concerns of regimental life and felt himself stripped of liberty and bound in one narrow, fixed frame — he experienced the same sense of peace, of moral grounding, of being at home in his proper place, as he had felt under his parents' roof. Gone was all the chaos of the wider world, where he didn't know where he belonged and made wrong decisions; gone was Sonya, with whom he needed to have — or not have — an explanation; gone was the possibility of going here or there; gone were those twenty-four hours a day that could be spent in so many different ways; gone was that enormous crowd of people, none of them closer or more distant than any other; gone were those uncertain, murky money matters with his father, and any thought of that terrible debt to Dolokhov. Here in the regiment everything was clear and simple. The whole world was divided into two unequal parts: one was the Pavlograd regiment; the other was everything else — and the rest was none of his concern. In the regiment, everything was defined: who was a lieutenant, who a captain, who was a good fellow and who wasn't, and above all, who was a comrade. The canteen keeper gave you credit; your pay came every four months; there was nothing to figure out or decide — you just had to avoid doing anything considered bad in the Pavlograd regiment and, when given an order, do exactly what was clearly and plainly commanded — and all would be well.

Having re-entered the fixed world of regimental life, Rostov felt the same joy and relief a tired man feels on lying down to rest. Life in the regiment during this campaign was all the pleasanter because, after his loss to Dolokhov — for which, despite all his family's consolation, he could not forgive himself — he had resolved to atone by serving not as before, but truly well, and by being a perfectly first-rate comrade and officer — in short, a splendid man altogether. This seemed so difficult out in the world, but so achievable in the regiment.
After his losses, he had resolved to repay his parents within five years. He received ten thousand rubles a year but now decided to take only two thousand and leave the rest for the debt.

The Russian army, after repeated retreats, advances, and battles at Pultusk and Preussisch-Eylau, was now concentrated near Bartenstein, awaiting the Emperor's arrival and the start of a new campaign.

The Pavlograd regiment, which belonged to the force that had served in the 1805 campaign, had been brought up to strength in Russia and arrived too late for the first engagements. It had fought neither at Pultusk nor at Preussisch-Eylau, and when it joined the army in the field during the second half of the campaign, it was attached to Platov's division.

Platov's division was operating independently of the main army. Several times units of the Pavlograd regiment had exchanged fire with the enemy, taken prisoners, and once even captured Marshal Oudinot's carriages. In April the Pavlograds had been stationed for several weeks near a completely ruined and deserted German village.

A thaw had set in — it was muddy and cold, the ice on the river was breaking up, and the roads had become impassable. For days on end, neither food for the men nor fodder for the horses had been delivered. Since no transports could get through, the men scattered through the abandoned villages searching for potatoes, but found hardly any of those either.

Everything had been eaten up and the inhabitants had fled. Those who remained were worse off than beggars, with nothing left to take. Even the soldiers — usually pitiless enough — often gave them the last of their own rations instead of taking from them.

The Pavlograd regiment had lost only two men wounded in battle but had lost nearly half its strength to hunger and disease. In the hospitals death was so certain that soldiers with fevers or the swelling caused by bad food preferred to stay on duty; they dragged their legs to the front line rather than go to the hospitals. When spring came, the soldiers found a plant just pushing through the ground that looked like asparagus. They called it "Mashka's sweet root" for some reason. It was very bitter, but they roamed the fields digging it up with their sabers and eating it, though they'd been ordered not to, since it was poisonous. That spring a new disease broke out — swelling of the arms, legs, and face — which the doctors attributed to eating this root. But despite everything, the men of Denisov's squadron ate mainly "Mashka's sweet root," because it was now the second week that the last biscuits were being rationed out at half a pound per man, and the potatoes they'd received had sprouted and frozen.
The horses had also been fed for two weeks on straw pulled from thatched roofs and had become terribly thin, though still covered with tufts of matted winter fur.

Despite this deprivation, soldiers and officers went on living as usual. Despite their pale, swollen faces and ragged uniforms, the hussars formed up for roll call, kept things in order, groomed their horses, polished their weapons, brought in roof straw instead of fodder, and gathered around the caldrons for dinner — from which they rose still hungry, joking about their wretched food and their hunger. As always, in their spare time they lit bonfires and stripped down to warm themselves by the flames, smoked, picked out and roasted sprouting rotten potatoes, and told stories of Potemkin's and Suvorov's campaigns, or tales of Alyosha the Sly or the priest's hired man Mikolka.

The officers, as usual, lived two or three to a room in roofless, half-ruined houses. The senior officers tried to gather straw and potatoes — food for the men in general. The junior officers occupied themselves as before, some playing cards (there was plenty of money, though no food), some with more innocent games like quoits and skittles. The overall course of the campaign was rarely discussed, partly because nothing definite was known, partly because there was a vague sense that things were going badly.

Rostov lived as before with Denisov, and since their furlough they had become closer than ever. Denisov never mentioned Rostov's family, but by the tender friendship his commander showed him, Rostov could tell that the older hussar's hopeless love for Natasha played a part in deepening their bond. Denisov clearly tried to keep Rostov out of danger as much as possible, and after each action he greeted his safe return with obvious joy. On one of his foraging expeditions, in a deserted, ruined village where he had come looking for food, Rostov found a family — an old Pole and his daughter with a baby in her arms. They were half-clothed, starving, too weak to walk, and had no way of getting a carriage. Rostov brought them to his quarters, put them in his own lodging, and kept them for several weeks while the old man recovered. One of his comrades, talking about women, began teasing Rostov, saying he was shrewder than any of them and that it wouldn't be a bad idea to introduce the pretty Polish girl he'd rescued. Rostov took the joke as an insult, flared up, and said such unpleasant things that Denisov could barely prevent a duel. When the officer had left, Denisov — who didn't himself know what Rostov's relationship with the Polish girl might be — began scolding him for his hot temper, and Rostov replied:
"Say what you like. She is like a sister to me, and I can't tell you how it hurt me... because... well, for that reason."
Denisov patted him on the shoulder and began rapidly pacing the room without looking at Rostov, as he always did in moments of deep feeling.
"Ah, what a crazy breed you Rostovs are!" he muttered, and Rostov noticed tears in his eyes.
